authors: Branch, F., Santana, I. & Hegde, J.
title: Biasing influence of 'mental shortcuts' on diagnostic decision-making: Radiologists can overlook breast cancer in mammograms when prior diagnostic information is available
relevance: Measures the cost of showing an expert interpreter a prior alongside the current image: anchoring rates of 38.3% for low-experience readers and 28.3% for the most experienced, with trained radiologists sometimes ignoring task-relevant image evidence entirely once anchoring information is present. That is the risk our paired photo-interpretation design takes on, and the direction is the dangerous one - anchoring suppresses apparent change, biasing a canopy-trend estimate toward zero exactly where the policy question lives. Expertise reduces it but does not remove it, so a single expert interpreter is not a mitigation.

title: Land use/land cover change detection combining automatic processing and visual interpretation
relevance: Argues the opposite failure to anchoring, from our own field: classifying each date INDEPENDENTLY generates FALSE CHANGE, and an interdependent or cascading protocol - classify the first date, carry the labels forward, edit only where change is seen - yields consistent maps without spurious transitions. Read together with the anchoring literature it defines the real trade-off in our Phase 3 response design: independent reading adds false change (variance, and it destroys the paired estimator's precision advantage), while cascading adds anchoring (bias toward stability). Neither is free, and the choice must be made deliberately rather than by default.
